about.title: Ontario Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: A fall rarely feels like a legal matter in the moment. You are embarrassed, maybe shaken, and mostly trying to get back up. In Ontario, those moments happen in grocery aisles, apartment stairwells, parking structures, and along the storefronts of Euclid Avenue, anywhere a property owner let a hazard sit unaddressed. Under California premises liability law, that last part matters most. To hold an owner responsible, you generally have to show they knew about the hazard, or reasonably should have, and failed to fix it or warn you. Lawyers call this "notice," and proving it usually comes down to evidence that disappears quickly: surveillance footage, incident reports, and the condition of the floor or walkway that day. LawProactive is a free service, not a law firm. We connect people hurt on someone else's property in San Bernardino County with an independent personal injury attorney who handles these claims on contingency, so there is no fee unless there is a recovery. Reaching out early gives that attorney a real chance to request the footage before it is overwritten.

whyChoose.title: Why Ontario Residents Turn to LawProactive After a Fall

items.title: Attorneys who know how to prove notice
items.desc: California requires proof that the owner knew or should have known about the hazard. The independent attorneys in our network know which records, cleaning logs, and prior complaints tend to show that.

items.title: Fast action on surveillance video
items.desc: Many Ontario stores, warehouses, and complexes overwrite camera footage within days. Getting an attorney involved quickly means a preservation request can go out before the evidence is gone.

items.title: Honest guidance on deadlines and shared fault
items.desc: You generally have two years to file, but far less if a public entity owns the property, and California's pure comparative fault rule means being partly at fault does not bar a claim. A network attorney can explain how both apply to your situation.

items.question: I fell on a city sidewalk or at a public building in Ontario. Is the process different?
items.answer: Yes, and the timing is the biggest difference. When the property belongs to the City of Ontario, San Bernardino County, or another government agency, California generally requires a written claim within six months of the injury, well before the usual two-year deadline. Missing that window can end the case regardless of how clear the hazard was, so it is worth speaking with an attorney right away.

items.question: The store says I should have watched where I was walking. Does that end my claim?
items.answer: Not under California law. The state follows pure comparative fault, meaning a court can assign a percentage of responsibility to you and still hold the owner accountable for their share. Your recovery would be reduced by your percentage, not eliminated. An independent attorney can push back on attempts to shift all the blame onto you.

items.question: What should I do in the first few days after a fall in Ontario?
items.answer: Photograph the exact spot, the hazard, your footwear, and any missing warning signs before the scene changes. Ask the business for an incident report and, in writing, request that they preserve any surveillance video. Get medical care even if the pain seems minor, since falls often reveal fractures or head injuries later. Then reach out so we can connect you with an attorney who can take over the evidence work.
